profile.description:
Hi there! I'm Maija, the founder of Freely Forward Bodywork. As an equine massage therapist, my focus is on enabling your horses’ comfort and performance through the use of massage therapy and stretching techniques. I aim to work with you and enable your horse to perform to its full potential, by analysing and assessing posture, movement, and skeletal function.

From providing a range of services to forming a treatment plan that is an integral part of my approach to treating the whole body, to offering online courses where you can learn effective techniques on how to treat your horse yourself, Freely Forward Bodywork is your go-to hub for equine wellness and performance.

Check out our brand new podcast, NO BUCKS GIVEN, where we have honest conversations about the horse industry with industry professionals about the hard truths around what matters most, how to best advocate for our horses. Subscribe here or anywhere you get podcasts!

If your horse feels heavy in your hands, braces against contact, or can't seem to reach forward and down no matter how much you soften, they may be stuck right where the neck meets the withers. Here's an easy technique that can make a big difference. Stand at the shoulder, place a hand on either side of the withers, and slowly rock them side to side. Just shift your own body weight back and forth and let the horse gently move with you. This loosens the deep muscles at the base of the neck, the spot that gets locked when a horse spends every ride bracing through the thoracic sling. Most horses will drop, stretch, and start reaching forward within a minute or two. It's best to do this when your horse is standing square, and repeat it a few times before you get on.  Follow me for more happy horse hacks!

Pro tip: Before you put a hand on the sacroiliac region, evaluate the pelvis. An imbalanced pelvis translates directly into the SI and lumbar, and if you skip that step you're chasing soreness instead of the imbalance driving it. I like to start with Pulse PEMF in the area. It improves microcirculation and warms the tissue so it's actually ready to release when you move into myofascial work. From there, gluteus medius is one of the first places I go. Then into the lumbar spine to decompress, or a sacral float. And do NOT skip the hamstrings. The biceps femoris ties into the sacrosciatic ligament, which is what makes it matter to the SI. Once you learn the anatomy and how it all ties together, knowing how to sequence your sessions will stop feeling like guesswork and look more like a roadmap. If you want to learn how to evaluate each horse as an individual and be confident coming up with a session plan to help each horse feel their absolute best, click the link in my bio and learn more about what makes my professional certification program different from others out there.

Here's what I actually see when I work on horses who are described as cold backed: A back that's tight, reactive, and genuinely uncomfortable when pressure is applied. That's not a quirk. That's a pain response. Signs your horse might be back sore: → Hollows or dips away when you mount → Pinned ears or tail swishing when you groom or tack up → Struggles to collect or in the canter and over jumps The back is the highway for energy to move through your horse's body. When it's not functioning the way it should, you'll start to see restrictions pop up in other areas of your horse's body and start a pain cycle. Click the link in my bio and I'll send you my free body mapping training so you can check your horse's back yourself today.

Before you say you can't make a living working with horses, read this first. I hear this all the time. "I wish I could work with horses but you can't make real money doing it." I want to challenge that, because I've seen too many talented, dedicated people talk themselves out of a career they would have loved, based on an assumption that just is not true. Equine bodywork practitioners make real money. They build client bases with retention. They create businesses that fit their lives instead of the other way around. And in most markets, they're not competing with a dozen others, they're filling a genuine gap. The ceiling on what you can build in this field is higher than you think, and the barrier to entry is lower than most horse careers. You don't have to believe me. Just look at my free guide first and you decide. Click the link in my bio and I'll send it to you! #horse #equinebodywork #horsesontiktok

Meet Jessica!  My 3rd graduate of the Freely Forward Equine Bodywork Certification!                                                                                                                    A bit about Jess, in her own words-  I’m Jessica Jurica, owner of Bloom & Balance Equine Bodywork, serving horses and their people throughout Blacksburg and surrounding Southwest Virginia communities. My approach to equine bodywork is individualized and centered on listening to the whole horse. I have a special interest in working with sensitive, shy, and guarded horses, creating sessions where each horse can feel safe, heard, and supported. My own horse, Daisy, is the inspiration behind Bloom & Balance. Learning to listen more closely to what she was communicating through her body led me to Freely Forward Bodywork and ultimately shaped the way I approach every horse I work with today. Every horse has a story to tell. I’m grateful to be part of it. Follow along on Instagram @bloomandbalanceequine or Facebook at Bloom & Balance Equine Bodywork, and learn more at bloomandbalanceequine.com

A poor topline gets blamed on fitness and feed more than almost anything else. And yes, nutrition and conditioning are important BUT here's what I want you to also consider: A horse can NOT build topline over a back that's in pain. When the back is sore, horses brace to protect themselves instead of engaging the muscles properly. They literally cannot use their topline correctly. So before you add another supplement or change your training, ask: → Is my horse's back reactive to palpation? → Does my saddle fit properly? → Is there tension through the lumbo-sacral area or hips? Address the pain first, THEN build the muscle. Not sure how to tell if your horse is in pain? Click the link in my bio and I'll send you my free equine body mapping guide so you know exactly how to check.

The horse who can't stand still is telling you something. Before you get into more advanced bodywork, try this rocking technique. It stimulates the vestibular system in the inner ear, which activates the parasympathetic response. Think about why a rocking chair settles a person, or why a mom rocks her baby. You're not convincing the horse to relax, you're giving their body a familiar signal that it is actually safe to. It isn't just for the anxious ones. Some of the most locked up horses I see aren't spooky at all, they're just braced from poll to tail and holding a pattern their nervous system forgot how to release. Rocking interrupts that. My favorite spot is the back. Put the pads of your fingers in the divot along the spine, then rock your own body slowly and let the movement travel into them. Start gentler than you think you need to. If they soften and ask for more, give them more. This is what I mean when I say you can help horses right now. It comes down to your hands and your willingness to let the horse lead. Everything else builds from there. If you want to make equine bodywork your full time job, comment CAREER and I'll send you the information.

Meet Jordan Sater, My Second Graduate! ✨ I am proud to introduce Jordan Sater of Second Flight Equine, my second graduate of the Freely Forward Equine Bodywork Certifiation. A little personal story - on my first day of the very first certification clinic I taught, Jordan got there before anyone else. I was incredibly, incredibly nervous and running around frantically, and said something to her along the lines of "...I just want to do a really good job for you guys" to which she responded "we're all here to learn, and we're going to learn together". That moment of kindness took a huge weight off my shoulders, and I've always been so thankful to her for it. I've admired her hard work in completing the program, as she balanced it with a full time job and owning horses, but still graduated at her second clinic with flying colors. She's exactly the kind of horsewoman I created this program for - hard working, intelligent, and passionate about helping horses through bodywork.  Jordan is now serving Southern Maryland and Southern Virginia, with travel available by request. Follow her @SecondFlightEquine to see her bodywork journey. Congratulations Jordan! I couldn't be prouder! 🎓🐴

The jaw is one of the most overlooked areas in equine bodywork and one of the most important. Here's what TMJ tension can look like: → Fighting the bit or bridle → Sticking their tongue out when they're ridden → One-sided stiffness through the neck → Trouble with contact or collection → Head tossing or resistance to bridling Here's what most people don't realize: tension in the jaw impacts functionality in the poll, the neck, and even the hind end. The TMJ has an incredible amount of nerves coming out of it and surrounding it that effect proprioception, and the rest of the body.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   Here are some things you can do to help your horse's TMJ:  - Get dental care for your horse every year or more often - Have their bit and bridle fitted by a professional fitter                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              - Make sure their noseband isn't too tight- this is an easy, but very important one! There should always be two fingers of room between the noseband and your horse's nasal bone.  -Try equine myofascial release to release fascial restrictions in the TMJ - this sounds intimidating, but it is really easy!

pages.excerpt: Shop Courses & Bundles Get Certified My Website FAQ User Library About Contact Log In Hello, I'm Maija Liisa Luttinger. As an equine massage therapist, my focus is on enabling your horses’ comfort and performance through the use of massage therapy and stretching techniques. I aim to work with you and enable your horse to perform to its full potential, by analysing and assessing posture, movement, and skeletal function. From providing a range of services to forming a treatment plan that is an integral part of my approach to treating the whole body, to offering online courses where you can learn effective techniques on how to treat your horse yourself, Freely Forward Bodywork is your go-to hub for equine wellness and performance. My Story I launched my business Freely Forward Bodywork in 2020 with the goal of helping riders and horses overcome the obstacles in their own bodies. I’m dedicated to helping each pair achieve peak performance by working in cooperation with their team of vets, farrier, saddle fitter, and coach. I now provide bodywork services to horses and riders across Eastern Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey, Maryland, Florida, and Iowa and treasure each horse and rider I work with. While my focus is bodywork in the muscular system, I try to get a comprehensive picture of the horse through my observation and consultation with you as the owner/rider. In a session, I watch and evaluate your horse on the ground and, at times, under saddle. In certain cases, riding your horse myself could give me insight into what you are feeling under saddle and, as a result, help me focus my efforts. By the end of the session, I can recommend stretches, exercises, and dressage training to continue your horse’s improvement. As a horse person, I have varied experience in dressage, eventing, western, and hunters, but throughout all disciplinary focuses I have been drawn to alternative methods for making my equine partner feel their best. After I moved from the Midwest to the East Coast at 19, I dove into the study of massage. I researched and learned from equine professionals while I was running an upper level eventing barn before adding human massage to my repertoire through Massage Therapy School where I became a Licensed Massage Therapist.
